newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Buthelezi backs pact with Mandela's ANC.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Buthelezi backs pact with Mandela's ANC.

text.p: South Africa's top black opposition leader, Mangosuthu Buthelezi, on Sunday backed unity with the ruling African National Congress (ANC), long the arch foe of his Inkatha Freedom Party.
"I do not see why it should not happen," Buthelezi said in an interview with South Africa's Sunday Times newspaper, adding it would be "an ideal thing".

The ruling party welcomed the remarks, saying it hoped this would serve to further the search for enduring peace in the Zulu heartland of KwaZulu-Natal where over 14,000 people have died in political feuding since 1984.
But ANC spokesman Ronnie Mamoepa was noncommittal on whether this would lead to closer ties or even a possible merger between the two parties.
"The ANC gives in unequivocal support to all current efforts aimed at achieving peace and stability in the province of KwaZulu-Natal," he told Reuters.

"Whether these peace efforts will lay a basis for a further advancement and cooperation between the two organisations will be left to the constitutional structures and constituencies of both organisations to decide," Mamoepa said.

Buthelezi, an ANC member in the 1960s who broke with the movement in 1979 over its commitment at the time to armed struggle, said the ANC and Inkatha had been driven apart by differences that were "not really necessary".
"There was a difference in strategy, not ideology," he said.
"I don't apologise for the fact that I come from the ANC stable."

ANC national chairman Jacob Zuma and his Inkatha counterpart Ben Ngubane are in the forefront of a peace initiative which has seen a significant thawing in relations between the parties over the past few months.

Buthelezi's support for the peace initiative is crucial but a political analyst based in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, Buthelezi's traditionalist Zulu powerbase, said the comments could not be interpreted as a major step forward.

"Buthelezi's words, to me, are on the vague and lukewarm side. They don't represent a sharp change or a sign of progress," Alexander Johnston, politics professor at the University of Natal, told Reuters.
